definition:
The Bible's teaching on work begins before sin. God himself works: Genesis describes creation as his work and his rest from it (Genesis 2:2-3), and Jesus says, “My Father is at His work, and I too am working” (John 5:17). Human beings, made in God's image, are given work as part of their calling. God places the man in the garden “to cultivate and keep it” (Genesis 2:15), so work belongs to creation, not to the curse. The fall does not bring work into the world; it makes work painful, frustrating, and often futile, and it opens the way for exploitation, idleness, and the worship of one's own achievements. So the Bible's law, prophets, and wisdom speak constantly about honest labor, fair wages paid on time, the protection of workers, and the rest that sets a limit to work. The New Testament calls believers to do whatever work they do “for the Lord and not for men” (Colossians 3:23), and it promises that labor “in the Lord is not in vain” (1 Corinthians 15:58). This study treats work and vocation; the weekly rest has its own study (Sabbath), as do money and possessions (Wealth and Possessions).

The Hebrew verb ʿavad covers a remarkable range: to work or till the ground, to serve a master, and to serve or worship God. It is the word for the man's work in the garden (Genesis 2:15), for Israel's forced labor in Egypt (Exodus 1:13-14), and for the service Israel was freed to give the LORD (Exodus 8:1). The context decides the sense; the range does not mean that every use carries all three. Its partner in Genesis 2:15, shamar, means to keep, guard, or watch over. Melakhah is work or craft, the word used of God's own work in Genesis 2:2 and of the skilled work of the tabernacle's builders; ʿamal, frequent in Ecclesiastes, is toil or labor with a note of weariness. The word for ‘painful toil’ in Genesis 3:17, ʿitsavon, is the same word used for the woman's pain in childbirth in the previous verse. In Greek, ergon is work or deed and ergazomai to work; kopos is labor to the point of weariness, a word Paul uses for his own manual work and his ministry alike. Paul's word klēsis, ‘calling’, is chiefly God's call to salvation, but in 1 Corinthians 7:20 it comes close to the situation in which a person was called, which is how later Christians came to speak of ordinary occupations as callings. Jesus is called a tektōn (Mark 6:3), a builder or craftsman who worked in wood, stone, or both.
ot:
Genesis 1 presents God as a worker who makes, separates, names, and fills, and who then rests. Humanity, made in his image, is given a share in his rule: to “fill the earth and subdue it” (Genesis 1:28). Genesis 2 pictures the same calling in a gardener's terms. The earth has “no man to cultivate the ground” (Genesis 2:5), so God forms one and places him in Eden “to cultivate and keep it” (Genesis 2:15). The man's naming of the animals (Genesis 2:19-20) is itself work: the patient ordering of a world. Then comes the fall. The ground is cursed, and the man will eat of it “through toil” and “by the sweat of your brow” until he returns to dust (Genesis 3:17-19). The curse does not create work; it bends it, so that labor now meets resistance, frustration, and death. Genesis 4 shows the double result. Cain, a worker of the ground, kills his brother and becomes a restless wanderer who builds a city, and yet among his descendants arise herdsmen, musicians, and metalworkers (Genesis 4:20-22), the beginnings of culture. Babel shows the same skill turned to self-glorification: “that we may make a name for ourselves” (Genesis 11:4).

Israel's story begins in forced labor. The Egyptians made the Hebrews' lives “bitter with hard labor in brick and mortar” (Exodus 1:14), and the exodus is God's liberation of workers from a system that treated them as tools. At Sinai, work is ordered by the command, “Six days you shall labor and do all your work” (Exodus 20:9), and bounded by a Sabbath that extends to servants, foreigners, and animals; Deuteronomy grounds it in Israel's memory, “Remember that you were a slave in the land of Egypt” (Deuteronomy 5:15). The same book of Exodus describes Bezalel as the first person in the Bible said to be filled with “the Spirit of God”, and the gift is “skill, ability, and knowledge in all kinds of craftsmanship” (Exodus 31:3). Artistic and manual work are thus honored as gifts of the Spirit. The law protects workers: wages are not to be held overnight (Leviticus 19:13), and a poor hired hand, Israelite or foreigner, must be paid “each day before sunset, because he is poor and depends on them” (Deuteronomy 24:15). Even the working ox is not to be muzzled (Deuteronomy 25:4). Gleaning laws left the edges of the harvest for the poor, who had to gather it by their own work (Leviticus 19:9-10; Ruth 2).

The historical books show work turned to good and evil ends. Solomon's temple is built by skilled craftsmen, including Huram (also called Hiram) of Tyre (1 Kings 7:13-14), but Solomon also imposed forced labor, and the people's plea to lighten that “heavy yoke” split the kingdom (1 Kings 12:4). After the exile the rebuilding of Jerusalem's wall is recorded as a common labor of priests, goldsmiths, merchants, and families, and it succeeded because “the people had a mind to work” (Nehemiah 4:6). The wisdom books look at work from every side. The psalmist sees daily labor as part of creation's order, “Man goes forth to his work and to his labor until evening” (Psalm 104:23), and prays, “establish the work of our hands” (Psalm 90:17), while warning that “Unless the LORD builds the house, its builders labor in vain” (Psalm 127:1). Proverbs sends the sluggard to learn from the ant (Proverbs 6:6-11), prizes skill (Proverbs 22:29), and praises the capable woman whose trade, weaving, and planting feed her household (Proverbs 31:13-24). Ecclesiastes is the Bible's most searching book about work. The Teacher hates his toil because he must leave it to someone who may be a fool (Ecclesiastes 2:18-19) and finds much of it “futile”, yet he concludes that “Nothing is better for a man than to eat and drink and enjoy his work” and that this is “from the hand of God” (Ecclesiastes 2:24).

The prophets judge a society by how it treats its workers. Jeremiah pronounces woe on the king who builds his palace “by unrighteousness” and “makes his countrymen serve without pay” (Jeremiah 22:13). Amos exposes merchants who resent the Sabbath because it interrupts their cheating (Amos 8:4-6), and Malachi lists those “who defraud laborers of their wages” among those God will judge (Malachi 3:5). The prophets' hope, in turn, is a world where work is fruitful and just. Swords become “plowshares” (Isaiah 2:4), and in the new heavens and new earth God's people “will build houses and dwell in them” and “will not labor in vain” (Isaiah 65:21-23). The Old Testament's vision of the end is not idleness but work set free from the curse.
nt:
The Son of God spent most of his earthly life as a manual worker. His neighbors in Nazareth asked, “Isn't this the carpenter”, referring to the trade of a tektōn (Mark 6:3), and Matthew calls him “the carpenter's son” (Matthew 13:55). He called fishermen and a tax collector from their work, and his parables are full of work: sowers and harvesters, shepherds, stewards, vineyard owners and day laborers, a woman sweeping for a lost coin. In the parable of the talents, faithful work with what the master entrusted is rewarded with the words “Well done, good and faithful servant” and with greater responsibility (Matthew 25:21). In the parable of the workers in the vineyard, those hired at the eleventh hour receive the same denarius as those who bore “the scorching heat of the day”, and the owner answers the grumblers, “are you envious because I am generous?” (Matthew 20:12, 15). The parable is about grace in the kingdom, not a wage policy, but it assumes that the day's wage is a livelihood. Jesus also speaks of his own mission as work: “My food is to do the will of Him who sent Me and to finish His work” (John 4:34), and in his prayer before the cross, “I have glorified You on earth by accomplishing the work You gave Me to do” (John 17:4). To the weary he offers rest: “Come to Me, all you who are weary and burdened” (Matthew 11:28).

The early church worked with its hands. Paul supported himself as a tentmaker alongside Aquila and Priscilla (Acts 18:3), and he reminded the Ephesian elders that “these hands of mine have ministered to my own needs” (Acts 20:34). He defended the right of those who preach to be paid, citing Deuteronomy's unmuzzled ox and the Lord's own teaching (1 Corinthians 9:9-14; compare Luke 10:7), yet often set that right aside so as not to burden new churches. He urged the Thessalonians “to work with your own hands” so as to win the respect of outsiders and not depend on others (1 Thessalonians 4:11-12). When some stopped working, apparently expecting the Lord's return, he repeated his rule: “If anyone is unwilling to work, he shall not eat” (2 Thessalonians 3:10). The word he uses for their conduct, ataktōs, means ‘disorderly’ or ‘undisciplined’, and the rule concerns the unwilling, not those unable to work. Work also has a purpose beyond self-support. The former thief is to work “that he may have something to share with the one in need” (Ephesians 4:28).

The household codes address the workers of the ancient household, many of them slaves. Paul tells slaves to serve “as to the Lord and not to men” and masters to “give up your use of threats”, because both have a Master in heaven with whom “there is no favoritism” (Ephesians 6:7-9). Colossians generalizes the principle: “Whatever you do, work at it with your whole being, for the Lord and not for men” (Colossians 3:23), and masters must give their slaves “what is right and fair” (Colossians 4:1). Paul also tells slaves that if they can gain their freedom they should take it (1 Corinthians 7:21), and he sends Onesimus back to Philemon “no longer as a slave, but better than a slave, as a beloved brother” (Philemon 1:16). These texts do not endorse slavery as an institution, and Christians later found in them the seeds of its abolition, though the church was slow to act on them. James stands in the line of the prophets: “the wages you withheld from the workmen who mowed your fields are crying out against you” (James 5:4).

The New Testament also sets work within the hope of the age to come. Paul tells the Corinthians that the resurrection of the body means their labor “in the Lord is not in vain” (1 Corinthians 15:58), and he pictures the day of judgment as a fire that will test the quality of each builder's work (1 Corinthians 3:12-15). Creation itself, subjected to futility, waits to be freed from “its bondage to decay” (Romans 8:21). Hebrews speaks of “a Sabbath rest for the people of God” still to come (Hebrews 4:9). In Revelation those who die in the Lord “rest from their labors, for their deeds will follow them” (Revelation 14:13), and into the new Jerusalem “the kings of the earth will bring their glory”, “the glory and honor of the nations” (Revelation 21:24, 26). Interpreters differ on how much of human work carries over into the new creation, but the Bible's final picture is a city, the work of God that gathers the works of the nations, and a people of whom it is said, “His servants will worship Him” (Revelation 22:3), using a Greek verb, latreuō, that joins service and worship much as the Hebrew ʿavad does.

keyTexts.why: Before sin, God places the man in the garden to cultivate and keep it, so work belongs to the good creation.
The curse falls on the ground and makes work painful toil ending in death. Work is bent by the fall, not created by it.
Six days of work and a seventh of rest for everyone in the household, grounded in God's own pattern of work and rest.
Bezalel is filled with the Spirit of God for craftsmanship, honoring skilled and artistic work as a gift of the Spirit.
The poor hired worker, Israelite or foreigner, must be paid each day before sunset, because he depends on his wages.
Unless the LORD builds the house, its builders labor in vain. Work depends on God, and anxious overwork is not faith.
The ant teaches diligence and foresight, and laziness leads to want.
The honest confession that work can feel futile, joined to the conviction that finding enjoyment in work is God's gift.
The new creation is pictured as fruitful work, building and planting, without futility or loss.
The parable of the talents rewards faithful work with what the master entrusted and condemns fearful idleness.
The former thief works with his hands so that he can give to those in need, showing work's purpose beyond self-support.
Whatever work believers do is service to the Lord Christ, and masters owe their workers what is right and fair.
Paul's own example and his rule that anyone unwilling to work should not eat, addressed to believers who had stopped working.
Withheld wages cry out to the Lord of Hosts; the exploitation of workers is a sin God hears.
The glory and honor of the nations are brought into the new Jerusalem, a picture of human achievement purified and gathered to God.

history:
The early church inherited from the Greek and Roman world a low view of manual labor; Aristotle had held that the life of the mechanic or laborer was unfit for the virtue of a citizen, whose leisure was the condition of the good life. Christians, whose Lord had been a craftsman and whose apostle had made tents, pushed against that view, though not always consistently. The monastic movement made work a daily discipline. Augustine wrote On the Work of Monks (around 400) against monks who refused manual labor in the name of prayer, arguing from Paul's example that they should work with their hands. The Rule of Benedict (sixth century) ordered the monastery's day around prayer, reading, and manual work, warning that idleness is the enemy of the soul. At the same time a two-level view of the Christian life took hold. Eusebius of Caesarea, in his Demonstration of the Gospel (book 1, chapter 8), described two ways of life given by Christ: a higher, perfect life devoted wholly to God and set apart from marriage, property, and ordinary work, and a lower, permitted life for those who marry, farm, trade, and fight. Medieval theologians such as Thomas Aquinas ranked the contemplative life above the active, while still treating ordinary work as good and necessary.

The Reformation reframed the question. Luther taught that every Christian is called by God, not only priests, monks, and nuns, and that the ordinary stations of life, as parent, ruler, servant, farmer, or craftsman, are callings (Beruf) in which a person serves God by serving the neighbor. His Address to the Christian Nobility (1520) attacked the idea of a spiritual estate set above ordinary believers. Gustaf Wingren's study Luther on Vocation (Swedish 1942, English 1957) remains the standard account of this teaching. Calvin similarly taught that God assigns each person a calling as a post from which not to wander, which gives dignity to the humblest work. English Puritans developed the doctrine in works such as William Perkins's A Treatise of the Vocations or Callings of Men (published 1603) and Richard Baxter's A Christian Directory (1673), which distinguished the general calling to be a Christian from the particular calling to a trade and urged diligence in both. Max Weber's The Protestant Ethic and the Spirit of Capitalism (1904 to 1905) argued, in a thesis much debated since, that this Protestant ethic of disciplined work helped shape modern capitalism.

Industrialization raised new questions of justice. Leo XIII's encyclical Rerum Novarum (1891) defended the right to private property, the right of workers to form associations, and the principle that a wage must be enough to support a frugal and well-behaved worker; it became the foundation of modern Catholic social teaching. John Paul II, himself a former quarry and factory worker, wrote Laborem Exercens (1981), which argues that work is for the person and not the person for work, and that the dignity of work rests first on the worker who does it rather than on the kind of work done. In the Netherlands Abraham Kuyper's teaching that Christ claims every sphere of life encouraged Christians to see business, science, and art as fields of obedience. Dorothy L. Sayers's address Why Work? (1942) urged the church to value work for its own sake as creative service rather than only as a means to earn money or a setting for evangelism. Miroslav Volf's Work in the Spirit (1991) proposed understanding work through the gifts of the Spirit and the hope of the new creation, and a broad faith-and-work movement since has sought to recover the Reformation doctrine of vocation for ordinary believers, as in Timothy Keller's Every Good Endeavor (2012).

differ.view: Vocation as the neighbor's service in one's station
differ.body: In the Lutheran tradition, and among many who follow it, a vocation is the concrete place where God has put a person: family, workplace, community, and church. Its defenders hold that God himself works through these callings, feeding the world through farmers and bakers and caring for children through parents, so that the worth of work lies in the neighbor it serves rather than in any achievement that outlasts it. They point to Paul's instruction that each person should live the life the Lord assigned (1 Corinthians 7:17-24) and to the household codes' call to serve the Lord in ordinary duties. They are wary of language that makes work a project of building the kingdom, fearing it may burden workers with a task only God can do.

differ.view: Work as participation in the coming new creation
differ.body: Other Christians, drawing on the neo-Calvinist tradition, on Miroslav Volf, and on N. T. Wright's Surprised by Hope (2008), hold that good work done in the Lord will in some way be purified and carried into the new creation. They point to Isaiah 65, to the glory and honor of the nations brought into the new Jerusalem (Revelation 21:24-26), to Paul's promise that labor in the Lord is not in vain (1 Corinthians 15:58), and to Romans 8, where creation itself is set free rather than discarded. On this view the cultural mandate of Genesis 1:28 still stands, and work in science, art, business, and government can anticipate the world to come.

differ.view: Work as provisional service in a passing age
differ.body: Many Christians, including many evangelicals and those in the Anabaptist tradition, stress the discontinuity between this age and the next. They point to texts that describe the present world as passing away (1 Corinthians 7:31; 1 John 2:17), to Jesus' warnings against storing up treasure on earth, and to the fire that tests every builder's work (1 Corinthians 3:13). Ordinary work, on this view, is good and necessary and must be done faithfully and honestly, but its lasting worth lies in the love and obedience with which it is done and in the witness it gives, not in its products. Defenders fear that too much talk of redeeming culture can distract the church from the gospel.

differ.view: Religious vocation and the call to ministry
differ.body: Catholic and Orthodox Christians hold that while all work can be sanctified, God calls some to religious life or ordained ministry as a distinct and particular vocation, and many Protestants likewise speak of a call to pastoral ministry that requires inward conviction and the church's confirmation. Defenders point to Jesus' calling of the Twelve from their nets, to Paul's setting apart for the gospel (Romans 1:1), and to Paul's praise of undivided devotion (1 Corinthians 7:35). Other Protestants, following Luther closely, resist any language that places such callings above others, insisting that the pastor and the plumber serve the same Lord in different offices, equal in dignity before God.

errors:
The church has rejected the view that work is a curse, beneath the dignity of the spiritual, or merely a distraction from prayer. Scripture places work in the garden before the fall, fills a craftsman with the Spirit, and presents the Son of God working with his hands. It has also rejected, less consistently than it should have, the two-level Christianity in which only priests, monks, and missionaries do God's work while everyone else merely earns a living. Paul's instruction that whatever believers do is service to the Lord Christ applies to all of them.

Other distortions are subtle. Work becomes an idol when a person's identity and worth are measured by productivity, status, or achievement, the error of Babel's builders and the rich fool; the Sabbath command, Psalm 127, and Jesus' offer of rest all rebuke it. Idleness, the refusal of work by those able to do it, is the opposite error, which Proverbs and Paul address directly. A further distortion treats work only as a means to other ends, a paycheck or a platform for evangelism, and ignores the goodness of the work itself and of the neighbor it serves. The gravest error is the exploitation of workers. The law, the prophets, and James all hold that withheld wages, forced labor, and cheating cry out to God; any teaching that uses the call to diligence to excuse injustice to workers has turned Scripture against itself.
life:
This doctrine gives ordinary days their weight. Whether a person teaches, cleans, farms, codes, raises children, or nurses the sick, the work can be done as service to the Lord and love for the neighbor it touches. That means doing it honestly and well, refusing shortcuts that harm others, treating co-workers and those one manages with the fairness owed to people who share the same Master, and paying what is owed on time. It also means holding work with an open hand: working hard without being defined by it, resting because God rests, and trusting that the worth of a life does not depend on what it produces.

For many people work is also a place of frustration, unemployment, injustice, or exhaustion, and Scripture does not pretend otherwise. Ecclesiastes gives words for the feeling that everything is futile, the psalms pray for the work of our hands to be established, and Jesus offers rest to the weary. Christians hope for a world where no one will labor in vain, and they are called to work toward justice for workers now. The promise that labor in the Lord is not in vain means that faithful work, even when it seems to vanish, is not lost to God.
questions: Genesis places work in the garden before sin. How does that change the way you think about the ordinary tasks of your week?

Paul tells workers to serve as to the Lord and masters to give what is right and fair, while the prophets and James condemn withheld wages. What would it look like to apply both halves of that teaching where you work?
Ecclesiastes calls much of our toil futile, yet Paul says labor in the Lord is not in vain. How do you hold those two truths together in your own work?
